title: Elastic Cloud Serverless audit logs: Ship the trail to Observability or Security
summary: Ship Elastic Cloud Serverless audit logs to an Observability or Security project. Seven dashboards cover object changes, data access and failed sign-ins.
body_markdown:
[Log delivery](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/monitor/log-delivery) is now generally available (GA) in[Elastic Cloud Serverless](https://www.elastic.co/cloud/serverless) . This means you can ship the audit logs from any Serverless project into an Elastic Observability Serverless or Elastic Security Serverless project in the same organization. The logs include eight alerting rules and seven dashboards that cover saved object changes in[Kibana](https://www.elastic.co/kibana) , along with the space where each change happened, who read which[Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/elasticsearch) index, and who was denied. They also cover sign-ins and the credential behind each one. Five Ignore filters drop whole slices of the stream before it’s delivered, so you pay to keep only what you’ll investigate. This first release is project activity, which is the[audit trail](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/monitor/log-delivery/audit-trail) for Elasticsearch and Kibana on the source project.


## How log delivery ships your audit logs


You just pick the source and the destination. If you don’t need the full audit trail, you define what you want to ignore. Elastic does the rest and delivers the trail, encrypted in transit and at rest.


Any project type in the organization, including Search, Elasticsearch Vector


Database, Observability, or Security, can be a source. The destination must be an Observability or Security project in the same organization. (If the source is already one of those, it can send the audit logs to itself.)


The destination is where you analyze the audit logs and where you set how long to keep them. It can be in any region or on any cloud provider, but needs to be in the same organization.


Each source project sends its audit trail to the selected destination. If your compliance team or the security operations center (SOC) wants to have a single place to investigate, you can point several source projects at the same Observability or Security destination.


Ingest and retention of audit logs are billed on the destination project. You decide how long the evidence should stay by[modifying the retention duration](https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/lifecycle/data-stream/tutorial-update-existing-data-stream) on the target data stream directly, and that retention time is part of the bill.


If you leave the **Ignore** filters empty, every single event is delivered. That’s the highest-volume option, and a busy project feels it on the[Observability](https://www.elastic.co/pricing/serverless-observability) or[Security](https://www.elastic.co/pricing/serverless-security) bill. Adding **Ignore** filters ensures that matching events are dropped before being delivered, so those events don’t reach the destination and aren’t billed.


After you turn on log delivery, you can watch the ingest rate and how much storage you’re keeping, in the[AutoOps Storage Tier view](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/monitor/autoops/storage-tier-view-autoops-serverless) on the destination project:


*AutoOps Storage Tier, where you can visualize the ingest rate of your audit logs and how much you’re keeping* .


## What Elastic Cloud Serverless audit logs contain


This release delivers project-level activity; that is, Elasticsearch and Kibana on the source project, including index, template, and pipeline changes, data searches, reads and writes, and UI access. All events land in` logs-elastic_cloud.serverless_audit.otel-default` .


` service.name` separates the producers. Elasticsearch events use` serverless-elasticsearch` , and Kibana events use` serverless-kibana` . Every event carries` project.id` , so you can tell which project it came from, even when several sources share the same destination.


An SOC uses the same stream for sign-ins and access failures, and a compliance team can keep it as evidence of who changed what. Organization administration will also soon land on the same trail, with sign-ins, membership modifications, identity and access management (IAM) checks, and project settings changes.


## How to turn on audit log delivery


There are five steps to turning on log delivery for Elastic Cloud Serverless audit logs, and you need the Admin or Editor role on the source project:


1.


On the Elastic Cloud home page, find the source project and select **Manage** .


2.


In the navigation menu, select **Log delivery** .


3.


For **Audit trail** , choose the destination project. An Observability project works if that’s where your team already investigates, but a Security project is the better home for this log type.


4.


Select any **Ignore** filters you want, switch **Audit trail** to **Enabled** , and then click on **Save** .


5.


Click on **View dashboard** to slice and dice your audit trail.


*Turn on the audit trail: pick a destination, drop what you don’t need, and then open the dashboard.*


### Audit logging best practices: What to keep and what to drop


Each filter drops a slice of the stream before it’s delivered:


Ignore filter


What it drops


When to use it


Data searches and reads


Searches and read operations on your data


On a search-heavy project, unless you need evidence of who read the data


UI requests


Read-only clicks in Kibana; saved object changes are still delivered


When read-only clicks are noise


Data writes


Ingest and bulk write operations


When you want configuration and object changes without write volume


Successful sign-ins


Sign-ins that succeeded; failures are still delivered


When you only care about failed sign-ins


Routine user and role checks


Routine IAM role checks; unusual IAM events are still delivered


When you want the unusual IAM events, not every role check


It’s useful to start with ignoring data searches and reads, in addition to UI requests. You keep the changes but drop the search volume and UI clicks. When you need the full stream and can pay for it, leave every filter off.


## 8 alerting rules that catch credential attacks


An attacker working through credentials leaves a shape in the audit stream. It might be one identity failing over and over or one address failing against many identities in turn. We ship eight alerting rules that watch for those shapes.


Analysts already work this way. When an alert arrives, you open a dashboard and investigate from there. These eight rules cover the first step.


Four rules watch for credential attacks:


Rule


What triggers it


Password guessing


One identity fails to sign in at least 15 times in 10 minutes.


Password spray


One client Internet Protocol (IP) address fails against at least 10 identities in 15 minutes.


Credential stuffing


At least 30 failures across 10 identities and five public IP addresses in 10 minutes.


Successful sign-in after repeated failures


At least five failures followed by a success in the same 30 minutes.


Keep an eye on that fourth one. A run of failures ending in a success is what a break-in looks like from the outside, and it’s the only rule here that fires after the attacker is already in.


The other four watch where a credential originates:


Rule


What triggers it


Impossible travel


Two sign-ins at least 500 km apart at the same moment or faster than 800 km/h within six hours.


Sign-in from a new country


A known identity appears in a country that it hasn’t used in the last seven days.


Credential used from many places


Two countries in one hour or an API key seen from three public IP addresses.


First-seen identity


The first sign-in in seven days.


First-seen identity has a startup cost worth knowing about. It stays quiet until the audit stream is at least a day old, because until that time, it has nothing to compare against. If you turn on log delivery this morning, don’t expect it to fire this afternoon.


Each rule points to one or more dashboards, so you get the trigger from the alert and the surrounding context from the dashboard.


## Audit log dashboards on the destination project


Seven dashboards come with your Elastic Cloud Serverless audit logs on the destination project. The stream is searchable in Discover, too, but the dashboards are the reason to turn this on. Below, we look at three of them more closely.


### Kibana Object Forensics: Who changed a saved object


Kibana Object Forensics is the change log, noting creates, updates, and deletes on saved objects, along with who performed the modification, the object that was modified, and the space where it occurred. A deleted detection rule shows up here:


*Kibana Object Forensics, including who changed a saved object and where.*


### Elasticsearch Data Access: Who read which index


Elasticsearch Data Access answers who read what, including index families, the transport action they used, denied requests, and reads of system and hidden indices. If you want to know who searched which indices, leave **Ignore data searches and reads** off.


*Elasticsearch Data Access, including who read the data, and who was turned away.*


### Identity & Access: Who signed in and what failed


Identity & Access is the sign-in page, and it includes credential type, authentication realm, failed sign-ins, and denied access. API keys are listed on their own, so a busy key isn’t mistaken for the person who created it:


*Identity & Access, including who signed in, with what, and what failed.*


## What’s coming next for log delivery


Two more log types are coming to log delivery on Elastic Cloud Serverless, beyond the Elasticsearch and Kibana audit logs available today:


-


[Elasticsearch query logs](https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/elasticsearch-query-logs) emit one coordinator-level line per query


for Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL), Query DSL, SQL, Event Query Language (EQL), and Prometheus Query Language (PromQL).


-


[Kibana user activity logs](https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/dashboard-activity-logs-kibana) record how Kibana is used. Dashboards are the first app on that stream, including who viewed, edited, or deleted one, and how long they take to load.


Open a project in[Elastic Cloud](https://cloud.elastic.co/projects) , and turn on **Log delivery** .
